title: Venice-Bound ‘Meteorite,’ Debut Feature From Colombia’s Sebastián Múnera, Acquired by MoreThan Films (EXCLUSIVE)
full_text: Aug 23, 2026 1:35am PT Venice-Bound ‘Meteorite,’ Debut Feature From Colombia’s Sebastián Múnera, Acquired by MoreThan Films (EXCLUSIVE) By Leo Barraclough Plus Icon Leo Barraclough International Features Editor LeoBarraclough Latest Seth Rogen, Colman Domingo, Danny Boyle Join Speakers Lineup at Toronto Market Summit 2 days ago The Freyas, a New Awards Ceremony Celebrating Nordic Film and TV Talent, to Launch in Helsinki (EXCLUSIVE) 3 days ago Sundance Prizewinner Luke Lorentzen’s Documentary ‘Boatbuilders’ Boarded by Metfilm Sales Ahead of Venice World Premiere (EXCLUSIVE) 3 days ago See All Courtesy of Haus Kino, Entre Acto MoreThan Films has acquired Colombian filmmaker Sebastián Múnera ‘s film “Meteorite,” which will have its world premiere in Venice Critics’ Week (Sept. 2-12). The film follows Tefa and Nia, who live in a small town near the Magdalena River, where they raise Nia’s young nephew. Nia persuades Tefa to join her in smuggling cellphones into the regional prison. Their journey leads them through an extravagant amusement park built on the grounds of a drug lord’s former estate. Related Stories 'One Battle After Another' and 'Marty Supreme' Take Top Honors at Location Managers Guild International Awards “As they wander among water slides, verdant paths, and concrete dinosaurs, disquieting memories whisper in the summer heat. In a landscape where violence lingers beneath every surface, Tefa is drawn toward an inevitable encounter,” according to the synopsis. Popular on Variety Queralt Pons Serra, managing partner at MoreThan Films, said, “What excited us about ‘Meteorite’ from the beginning was the strength and singularity of Sebastián’s gaze. You can really feel his artistic background in the way he approaches images, spaces and textures, creating a world that is incredibly cinematic, beautiful and also deeply emotional. There is something very immersive and atmospheric about the film that stayed with us long after watching it.” Múnera is a Colombian visual artist and filmmaker. He was a resident at the Cité Internationale des Arts in Paris, invited by the Centre Georges Pompidou. His films have been selected at festivals such as IFFR Rotterdam, DOK Leipzig and FICCI Cartagena. He has received distinctions including the Humberto Solás Cine en Construcción Award and the International Symposium on Auteur Cinema Altiplano Incuba Award. “Meteorite,” his first fiction feature, was awarded at work-in-progress programs in Málaga and Cartagena. The producers are Sebastian Martinez, Mauricio S. Varma’s Sequel Titled ‘Zombie Reddy Nxt Lvl’ (EXCLUSIVE) By Naman Ramachandran Plus Icon Naman Ramachandran Latest Upendra Joins Cast as Teja Sajja, Shanaya Kapoor, Suparn S. The announcement, made on star Teja Sajja ‘s birthday, also confirms the film’s cast and creative team. The adventure zombie action-comedy marks the South Indian cinema debut of “Tu Yaa Main” star Shanaya Kapoor . Teja Sajja returns as the franchise’s zombie-slaying lead. Related Stories 'One Battle After Another' and 'Marty Supreme' Take Top Honors at Location Managers Guild International Awards Directed by Prasanth Varma, “Zombie Reddy” was released in 2021, and followed a game developer who must save his village after a scientist’s vaccine experiment unleashes a zombie outbreak. Popular on Variety Suparn S. Varma, known for Prime Video’s “The Family Man” Season 2, Netflix’s “Rana Naidu” and film “Haq,” directs the sequel from a story created by Prasanth Varma. Gowra Hari, whose scores powered “HanuMan” and “Mirai,” composes the music. Hussain Dalal, Prasanth Varma and Suparn S. Varma wrote the screenplay. T.G. Vishwa Prasad and Krithi Prasad produce for People Media Factory. The film will release in seven languages – Hindi, Telugu, Kannada, Tamil, Malayalam, Nepali and Japanese. “The biggest takeaway from my career is that cinema survives on audacity, not formulas,” Teja Sajja said. “When ‘Zombie Reddy’ was made, it was a calculated risk born out of a desire to break the monotony of conventional storytelling. I can’t thank the audience enough for embracing me as a zombie slayer and their unbridled curiosity and faith in what I do next. It’s the love that I’ve received over the years that pushes me to make brave choices. So here’s a promise to take the mayhem to a whole new scale in ‘Zombie Reddy Nxt Lvl.’ As I turn a year older, the zombies turn deadlier. With the audience validating everyone associated with the film, I’m all set to fight the dead onscreen like never before. It makes me very proud to be part of a team that wants to give viewers a grand, immersive spectacle that feeds their appetite for the extraordinary.” Suparn S. Varma said the goal was to surprise both himself and the audience with something unlike anything seen before. “Zombies have always been a fascinating expression of our worst catastrophes, and with this film, we wanted to take that idea to the next level,” he said. “We’ve taken the foundational brilliance that Prasanth Varma created and blown it wide open, building a never-seen-before zombieverse. It’s been an absolute treat to explore a genre with such enormous creative possibilities and collaborate with stalwarts who bring their own seasoned finesse to the film. Here’s wishing one of them – the audience’s superstar and favourite zombie slayer, Teja Sajja, a very happy birthday!” T.G. Vishwa Prasad said People Media Factory has always aimed to push the boundaries of commercial cinema. “‘Zombie Reddy Nxt Lvl’ is an epic adventure designed for a global audience, which is why we are releasing it from India to Japan,” he said. “Everything is next level right from the actors starring in it to the director, technicians, and music. title: Taylor Sheridan Accused of Stealing ‘Yellowstone’ Idea From TV Writer’s Pitch
full_text: × Skip to main content By Hilary Lewis Plus Icon Hilary Lewis Deputy Editor, East Coast hilarylewis Follow Sign Up View All August 22, 2026 8:30pm Gil Birmingham as Chief Rainwater and Mo Brings Plenty as Mo in season 5B of 'Yellowstone.' Paramount Network Taylor Sheridan , Paramount and NBC Universal are all being sued by a writer who says Sheridan stole her idea for a TV show and used it to create Yellowstone . In the suit, filed in the U.S. District Court for the Central District of California on Friday, TV writer and entertainment journalist Lauren J. Salkin claims she submitted a pilot script, show bible and pitch deck for a show called Sovereign Nation to Sheridan’s reps at his management company, Elevate Entertainment, which is also named as a defendant in the suit, in late 2016 and early 2017. Related Stories Business Mark Ruffalo Rejects Paramount's Claim His Anti-Merger Comments Were "Antisemitic": "My Views Should Never Be Interpreted as Hostility Toward Jewish People" Business Gavin Newsom Says Paramount Settlement Talks Happening in "Real Time," Signals He'd Like a Deal Sovereign Nation, which Salkin spent more than 10 years developing, is described in the complaint, which was viewed by The Hollywood Reporter , as a “dramatic television series centered on tribal governance, casino-driven economic power and a modern war over land and development.” Salkin alleges that she received a response from Elevate on Feb. 1, 2017 saying that Sheridan was “unavailable for TV projects.” “Within months, Paramount greenlit Sheridan’s Yellowstone ,” the complaint states. The show premiered on the Paramount Network on June 20, 2018 and later began streaming on Peacock. The suit says Yellowstone featured “specific expressive choices already embodied in Salkin’s materials” including “a tribal casino functioning as the institutional center of political and development power; a signature confrontation staged in the tribal chairman’s casino office over expansion beyond reservation boundaries; the use of trust land, the absence of zoning restrictions and a 99-year lease structure as the concrete mechanism for that expansion; and recurring master-plan imagery deployed to dramatize the struggle for territorial control.” Salkin also argues that Yellowstone followed several of her proposed casting recommendations for key roles in Sovereign Nation . “Copyright law does not protect the abstract idea of a Western, a land dispute, an Indian casino or a powerful family — and that is not Plaintiff’s claim,” the complaint states. “The infringement alleged here lies in the copying of Salkin’s particular expressive choices and their coordinated selection and arrangement.” The suit also notes that a senior HBO scripted TV executive who had reviewed materials for Sovereign Nation later told her he recognized similarities in Yellowstone . Salkin argues that the hit Kevin Costner-led series, which has spawned numerous spinoffs, “has generated billions of dollars” for the defendants, of which she “has received nothing.” Salkin is seeking damages and profits tied to alleged copyright infringement and injunctive relief preventing future infringement. “This is a classic David-versus-Goliath situation,” Salkin’s attorney Paul B. Lackey told THR . “She spent years putting together the specific and multi-layered framework for a story that has become the biggest streaming success of all time. She has watched the vast commercial success of this story that was stolen from her and decided that enough was enough. We will do everything in our power to get her justice.” Reps for Sheridan, Paramount, Elevate and NBCUniversal have not yet responded to THR ‘s request for comment. THR

title: ‘One Battle After Another’ and ‘Marty Supreme’ Take Top Honors at Location Managers Guild International Awards
full_text: Aug 22, 2026 8:22pm PT ‘One Battle After Another’ and ‘Marty Supreme’ Take Top Honors at Location Managers Guild International Awards By Isabelle Farina Plus Icon Isabelle Farina Latest Sonic the Hedgehog to Headline Fortnite’s ‘Override’ Season (Gaming News Roundup) 1 day ago Jaafar Jackson: ‘Michael’ Sequel Will Give ‘More Insight’ Into Child Abuse Allegations and ‘Let His Voice Be Heard’ 2 days ago CBS Sets ‘Daughters of 9/11’ Special for 25th Anniversary of Sept. 11 3 days ago See All ©Warner Bros/Courtesy Everett Collection “One Battle After Another” and “Marty Supreme” took top honors at the Location Managers Guild International (LMGI) LMGI Awarda. The LGMI Awards were handed out on Saturday night and honor the use of filming locations across motion pictures, television, commercials, film commissions, and special achievement categories. Paul Thomas Anderson’s “One Battle After Another” won outstanding locations in a contemporary feature film. It was shot across California’s Humboldt County, Sacramento, Stockton, Eureka, Arcata, San Diego and El Paso, Texas. Josh Safdie’s “Marty Supreme” won outstanding locations in a period feature film for its work across New York City, greater New York, the Hudson Valley, New Jersey and Tokyo. Related Stories 'One Battle After Another' and 'Marty Supreme' Take Top Honors at Location Managers Guild International Awards “Pluribus,” “Fallout” and “Black Rabbit” were the television winners. “Pluribus” was filmed in Albuquerque, New Mexico, Montana, Nevada, and Spain, and won outstanding locations in a contemporary television series. “Fallout,” shot in California’s Dumont Dunes, Mojave Desert, Antelope Valley and Santa Clarita,” won outstanding locations in a period television series. Filmed around New York City, including Brooklyn and Manhattan, “Black Rabbit” won outstanding locations in a tv anthology, movie or limited series. Popular on Variety Four-time Emmy-winning director and writer Vince Gilliga received the Eva Monley Award for his dedication to storytelling through location over his career and his most recent work on “Pluribus.” Mike Fantasia, location manager of films including “Top Gun: Maverick,” “Killers of the Flower Moon” and “Spider-Man: Homecoming” was presented the Lifetime Achievement Award. “Celebrating our LMGI winners was a truly remarkable experience,” Nancy Haecker, LMGI Awards Chair, said. “The ceremony was a powerful celebration of achievement, filled with inspiring moments and well-deserved recognition, beautifully capped by the genius of Vince Gilligan. Each of this year’s winners is incredibly deserving, and it was a distinct privilege to honor their talent, dedication, and outstanding contributions to our industry.” Winners list below. title: Simon Wiesenthal Center CEO Calls Out Mark Ruffalo For “Antisemitism” & “Demonization”
full_text: Skip to main content By Tom Tapp Tom Tapp Deputy Managing Editor More Stories By Tom Simon Wiesenthal Center CEO Calls Out Mark Ruffalo For “Antisemitism” & “Demonization” Bunny Levine Dies: Librarian Turned Actress Who Appeared In Everything From ‘Gilmore Girls’ To Adam Sandler Movies Was 97 Disney Inks Creator Content Deal With Dhar Mann Studios View All August 22, 2026 8:18pm Mark Ruffalo attends the AFI Awards in 2026 JC Olivera/PMC Just hours after Mark Ruffalo responded to Paramount ‘s accusations of antisemitism, the CEO of the Simon Wiesenthal Center issued a statement to Deadline on the subject. “Words matter, and so does the willingness to draw a line when legitimate debate gives way to antisemitic tropes,” wrote Jim Berk. Related Stories News Mark Ruffalo Blasts Paramount For Calling Him “Antisemitic” Over Merger Criticism: “Appalling And Fundamentally Dishonest” News Mark Ruffalo Notes Many “Were Afraid” To Sign Letter Opposing Paramount-Warner Bros Merger: “Not Unjustified” “We commend Paramount for speaking clearly and refusing to allow prejudice to masquerade as political or corporate criticism. At a time when antisemitism is too often minimized, rationalized or repackaged in more socially acceptable language, this kind of moral clarity matters.” The corporate criticism to which Berk refers is Ruffalo’s initial assertion about Paramount and the finacial support it receives from CEO David Ellison’s father, Watch on Deadline “This is the company that Larry Ellison is using to fund his son David’s Warner Bros acquisition,” wrote Ruffalo alongside a clip of the tech company’s executive vice chair Safra Catz discussing how they made some “really profoundly scary technology” available to the Israeli military amid the ongoing Israel-Hamas conflict. “These ‘really profoundly scary technologies’ will most likely be merged into one of the largest media conglomerates in the world and one day used on you. Look how she revels in what we now have come to see as a genocide, which was built on an apartheid system of oppression powered by Oracle.” He continued, “Larry Ellison will own most of ‘Para Bros’. Larry is a classic Oligarch. They are crushing workers and consolidating the wealth of the world for their own power and concentrated dominance.” In response, Paramount said in part, “We are, as always, troubled when antisemitic tropes are invoked in purported service of a business dispute,” said a spokesperson. “Words like ‘genocide’ and ‘apartheid,’ applied to a corporate transaction, aren’t just wrong — they’re a bridge too far, and they cheapen the very real suffering those words are meant to describe.” Wiesenthal CEO Berk said Ruffalo was conflating two issues. “Invoking Israel in an issue where it is completely irrelevant is a textbook case of obsession and demonization. Paramount was right to call it out.” Deadline has reached out to Ruffalo for comment and this post will be updated when one is received. title: Bunny Levine Dies: Librarian Turned Actress Who Appeared In Everything From ‘Gilmore Girls’ To Adam Sandler Movies Was 97
full_text: Skip to main content By Tom Tapp Tom Tapp Deputy Managing Editor More Stories By Tom Karoline Leavitt Announces Post-White House Job Simon Wiesenthal Center CEO Calls Out Mark Ruffalo For “Antisemitism” & “Demonization” Bunny Levine Dies: Librarian Turned Actress Who Appeared In Everything From ‘Gilmore Girls’ To Adam Sandler Movies Was 97 View All August 22, 2026 6:47pm Bunny Levine attends the L.A. Premiere of 'Thelma' in 2024 Getty Bunny Levine , a librarian who took early retirement and then began acting on such shows as Gilmore Girls and Shameless as well as two Adam Sandler films, has died, according to multiple reports. She was 97. Levine graduated from college in 1951 and became a school librarian in New Jersey, where she worked before deciding to try acting full time. Levine had wanted to perform since childhood. Related Stories Obituaries 2026 Deaths Photo Gallery: Hollywood & Media Obituaries News Kid Cudi Preparing To Film “F*ckin Gnarly” Followup To Directorial Debut ‘Doe’, Both Set For 2027 “I don’t know why. I don’t know that many of us could explain why — it’s just something,” she told her alma mater’s student newspaper, The Daily Evergreen , in 2025. “Maybe it’s in the genes.” Whatever it was, the diminutive actress (she was 4’10”) worked steadily on network television for the better part of four decades, mostly in single episode appearances as a character called “Old Lady,” Kindly Older Woman” or “Grandma.” Among the titles: As the World Turns, Law & Order, Chappelle’s Show, Everybody Loves Raymond, Las Vegas, Private Practice, Ugly Betty, Community, Criminal Minds, 2 Broke Girls, The Mindy Project, Fuller House and Mayans M.C. In film, one of her first appearances came in 1990’s Cadillac Man , starring Robin Williams and Tim Robbins. She was cast opposite Adam Sandler in Don’t Mess With the Zohan (as “Older lady in the salon”) and in an uncredited role as the main character’s grandmother in Sandy Wexler. Also on the big screen, Levine played a movie theater cashier in La La Land , Mrs. Grossman in Let Go and Mona opposite June Squibb in 2024’s Thelma . title: ‘National Treasure 3’ Is “Finally Real” and “We Have a Script,” Director Says
full_text: × Skip to main content By Lexi Carson Plus Icon Lexi Carson Associate Editor View All August 22, 2026 6:11pm From left: Diane Kruger, Justin Bartha and Nicolas Cage in 'National Treasure: Book of Secrets.' Walt Disney Pictures/Courtesy Everett Collection Get ready for another treasure hunt: A third National Treasure movie is happening, according to director Jon Turteltaub. Speaking at a live taping of the National Treasure Hunt podcast Friday night in Philadelphia, Turteltaub said, “It’s happening. You’re the first people I’ve said this out loud to. I have not said anything before this, but you deserve to have the scoop. It’s finally real. Now, it’s ‘Hollywood real,’ meaning things could happen. Nic [Cage] gets hit by a bus, there’s no National Treasure 3. If I get hit by a bus, there’s probably a National Treasure 3. Welcome to Hollywood.” Related Stories Business Disney Strikes Content Deal With Dhar Mann Studios TV ABC Sues FCC Over Threats to Broadcast Licenses in First Amendment Case “We finally have a script that I like,” he said before adding before revealing that Disney said, “OK, this sounds like a movie we can make.” The Hollywood Reporter reached out to Disney for comment and they declined. The first National Treasure film was released in 2004 and followed Cage as historian Ben Gates, who steals the Declaration of Independence to find a map to an ancient, rumored treasure before anyone else can get to it. Harvey Keitel, Jon Voight, Diane Kruger, Sean Bean, Justin Bartha and Christopher Plummer also starred in the film, which grossed $347 million at the global box office. The 2007 follow-up, National Treasure: The Book of Secrets , earned $459 million worldwide and added Helen Mirren, Ed Harris, Bruce Greenwood and Ty Burrell to the cast. The franchise later expanded to television with National Treasure: Edge of History , which premiered on Disney+ in 2022 but was canceled after one season. title: ‘Spa Weekend’ Review: Leslie Mann and Isla Fisher Go Underserved in a Lukewarm Bath of a Comedy
full_text: × Skip to main content By Angie Han Plus Icon Angie Han Television Critic ajhan Follow Sign Up View All August 22, 2026 5:21pm 'Spa Weekend' Black Bear Pictures Have you ever had the experience of booking a trip that promised to be a blissful getaway, only to find once there that you’re having…not the worst time, but definitely a disappointing one? That the food that looked so pretty online tastes bland in person, that the overstuffed pillows give you neck pains, that — come to think of it — there’s not really that much to do at this resort beyond linger beside a lukewarm pool? If so, the aura of letdown surrounding Spa Weekend , the latest outing from writer-directors Jon Lucas and Scott Moore, ought to feel familiar. On paper, it’s a variation on the “R-rated hijinks plus heartfelt emotion plus beloved cast” equation that’s worked so well for Bridesmaids and Girls Trip and Lucas and Moore’s own commercially successful though creatively uninspired Bad Moms . In execution, the hijinks feel awfully tame, the emotion shallow, the stars underserved. Related Stories Movies 'Insidious: Out of the Further' Hunts Down $3M in Box Office Previews Movies Anna Faris Reveals Melania Trump Joke Cut From 'Scary Movie' Spa Weekend The Bottom Line A likable cast let down by uninteresting hijinks. Release date: Friday, Aug. 21 Cast: Leslie Mann, Isla Fisher, Michelle Buteau, Anna Faris, Adam Demos, Dominic Ona-Ariki, Erika Heynatz Director-screenwriters: Jon Lucas, Scott Moore Rated R, 1 hour 37 minutes The premise is the title, not much more and not much less. On the occasion of her she’s-not-saying-which birthday, overworked Los Angeles lawyer Jane ( Leslie Mann ) books a two-night stay at a wellness retreat seemingly around Malibu, though the Australia-shot production avoids getting too geographically specific. (Wherever it is, the sunsets are very pretty.) Along with her for the ride are her two childhood besties — sweet-natured Sophie ( Anna Faris ), who’s withering under a boss so spoiled he can’t even buy his own Skittles, and hot-tempered Coco ( Michelle Buteau ), who’s working through a painful divorce while stubbornly not working through the anger management issues that led to it. The trip promises to be precisely the break all three of them desperately need but cannot ever seem to take, because as working moms pulled every which way by ailing parents, needy kids and demanding jobs, these women cannot imagine planning so much as a date night less than three months in advance. They could certainly never do something so self-indulgent as book a whole trip on a whim — except that that’s exactly what we’ve just seen them do, within five minutes of Coco floating the idea over brunch. I presume the whiplash-inducing speed with which the trio go from “Oh, I couldn’t possibly” to “We’ve booked the room” is meant to be aspirational: Here are women finally saying “screw it” to a society that demands they put everyone else first, and taking care of themselves for once! But it has the condescending effect of suggesting that their struggles were never real to begin with. The only thing ever actually holding them back, apparently, was their own lack of willpower. Well, that and, in some roundabout way, their lack of appreciation for the unwanted fourth member of their circle. Mel ( Isla Fisher ), who’s only scored a last-minute pity invite thanks to Sophie’s guilty conscience, is “the one woman all the others secretly cannot stand” — you know, that thing Spa Weekend assures us every female friend group always has. If you can’t identify who that might be in your own girl gang, maybe that’s because it’s you. Or maybe it’s because Spa Weekend has a habit of treating all its characters’ problems as universal and therefore inherently relatable and interesting. You can practically hear the “Am I right, ladies?” after every such observation. In fairness to Jane, Coco and Sophie, their distaste initially proves warranted. From the moment Mel bursts onto the property — boobs spilling out of her pushup bra, dildos spilling out of her suitcase, inappropriate language spilling out of her mouth — she brings nothing but chaos. When she’s around, a guided meditation session devolves into a shouting match, a chill evening into a cocaine-fueled rager, a short walk between spa treatments into, somehow, a wild golf cart chase. None of it is anything you haven’t seen before, and in Lucas and Scott’s ineffectual hands, none of it gets as nasty or raunchy or destructive as those descriptions suggest. What’s more, Mel can’t seem to stop meddling in her friends’ live. She swipes Sophie’s phone to scream at her shitty boss. She tricks Coco’s ex (Dominic Ora-Ariki’s Roger) into rushing to her side. She baldly propositions Adam Demos’ hot yoga instructor on Jane’s behalf (“Obviously she’s on the older side, but she’s got a porno body!”). Her behavior is upsetting and mortifying and potentially life-destroying to all her friends until it’s not, as Spa Weekend slowly but predictably gets around to the argument that the world needs Mels — the hot messes who force everyone else out of their miserable but societally approved ruts. It would be a very nice message, if not for the fact that the script undercuts it by keeping all its characters too vague and one-dimensional to care much about in any direction; I couldn’t even tell you what Coco does for a living or why Jane’s raising her kids alone. To the extent that there are any genuine chuckles or warm fuzzies to be found in Spa Weekend , it’s thanks to skills this talented core cast have deployed more effectively elsewhere. A pretty funny scene in which Jane tries very hard to pretend she’s not extremely turned on by Demos’ Kai giving her a hand massage called to my mind the even funnier ones of Mann smiling through her tears in Blockers . Coco’s smooth, sexy chemistry with Roger made me want to revisit Buteau’s winsome turn as a heartbroken stylist in Netflix’s Survival of the Thickest . Fisher earns most of the film’s few real laughs by channeling the upbeat yet unhinged energy that’s served her so well since her breakout in Wedding Crashers . Even Faris’ miscast turn as awkward, mousy Sophie served to remind me how much more delightful she is when she gets to go weird and messy, as in The House Bunny or Smiley Face . But the ability to occasionally evoke other, better projects does not a good film make. Spa Weekend has nothing fresh or insightful or even all that amusing to add to the familiar formula it’s borrowing — and for all its apparent good intentions, nothing much more meaningful to offer the overworked, overstressed moms of the world than the suggestion that maybe they could, like, try taking a vacation sometime. If this is what a big relaxing escape looks like, you’re better off saving the money and chilling at home. title: Mark Ruffalo Rejects Paramount’s Claim His Anti-Merger Comments Were “Antisemitic”: “My Views Should Never Be Interpreted as Hostility Toward Jewish People”
full_text: × Skip to main content By Hilary Lewis Plus Icon Hilary Lewis Deputy Editor, East Coast hilarylewis Follow Sign Up View All August 22, 2026 5:10pm Mark Ruffalo at the AFI Awards in January. Rodin Eckenroth/Getty Images for AFI Mark Ruffalo is rejecting Paramount ‘s claim that his recent comments highlighting the role Larry Ellison’s Oracle played in the Israel-Gaza war were “antisemitic.” “The accusation that I am antisemitic is appalling and fundamentally dishonest,” Ruffalo wrote on X Saturday morning . “Criticizing the actions of the Israeli prime minister, a military technology contract or the executives who supply it is not the same as criticizing Jewish people. This critical and necessary dialogue is then dishonestly framed as being anti-Israel. To be clear, my views come from my own political convictions and should never be interpreted as hostility toward Jewish people, for whom I have deep love and respect. Everything I know about acting, activism and humanism has been profoundly shaped by the Jewish friends, colleagues and loved ones who have been integral and family throughout every point of my life.” Related Stories Business Mark Ruffalo Links Paramount to Oracle's Israeli Military Ties. The Studio Calls Remarks "Antisemitic" Business Gavin Newsom Says Paramount Settlement Talks Happening in "Real Time," Signals He'd Like a Deal Ruffalo, a staunch opponent to Paramount’s $111 billion deal for Warner Bros. , had recently shared on social media a clip from 2024 of former Oracle chief Safra Catz talking about “profoundly scary technologies” Oracle had built as Catz was speaking about Oracle’s tech in relation to the Israel-Gaza war. Ruffalo went on to call the war a “genocide” that “was built on an apartheid system of oppression powered by Oracle.” He added in his Instagram story that these “profoundly scary technologies” “will most likely be merged into one of the largest media conglomerates in the world” and criticized the planned Paramount-WB merger, saying moguls “are crushing workers and consolidating the wealth of the world for their own power and concentrated dominance.” Paramount issued a lengthy reply in which the company called for the temperature of the debate to be lowered and called Ruffalo’s remarks “antisemitic.” “We are, as always, troubled when antisemitic tropes are invoked in purported service of a business dispute,” the Paramount rep stated. “Words like ‘genocide’ and ‘apartheid,’ applied to a corporate transaction, aren’t just wrong — they’re a bridge too far, and they cheapen the very real suffering those words are meant to describe. This doesn’t deserve a response in kind — and to be clear, we don’t tolerate prejudice of any kind, against anyone.” Paramount added, “We understand people feel strongly about this merger and are hopeful and expect that it will be judged based on the legal merits, not underlying bias. We’re asking for the same good faith we’re extending: less rhetoric, more understanding. Paramount’s future is being written for everyone who wants to make and watch great stories.” In his response Saturday, Ruffalo sought to make a distinction between his objections to the Israeli military and his views about the Jewish people. He also argued that the merger “has real consequences for real people and for the entire country” and deserved serious scrutiny, particularly given what the deal would mean for control of CNN, HBO and other Warner Bros. assets. “Scrutinizing the Ellisons, including Oracle’s business built on data, surveillance technology and government contracts and the serious threat to editorial freedom and the loss of a livelihood for thousands of families, is fair and necessary,” Ruffalo wrote. “The $111 billion deal would hand one family control over CNN, HBO and Warner Bros., backed in part by foreign money whose influence on editorial decisions has never been fully explained to the public. Lawmakers on both sides of the aisle have called for serious national security review, and regulators still haven’t given the public a real answer. Until they do, the merger shouldn’t move forward. Now is the time to dive boldly into all these issues, not step back or concede.” In his Instagram story about Oracle’s “profoundly scary technologies,” Ruffalo mentioned the ongoing antitrust lawsuit filed by 12 attorneys general, which Paramount said last week is the only thing stopping the deal from being done , now that the merger has been cleared by all global regulators. Still a number of officials, including California Governor Gavin Newsom , Attorney General Rob Bonta , California Democratic gubernatorial candidate Xavier Becerra and L.A. mayor Karen Bass , have expressed support for settlement talks, which Newsom said Friday were happening “in real time.” THR

title: Bunny Levine, Librarian Turned Actress in ‘Gilmore Girls,’ Thelma’ and ‘You Don’t Mess With the Zohan,’ Dies at 97
full_text: Skip to main content By Lexi Carson Plus Icon Lexi Carson Associate Editor View All August 22, 2026 4:40pm Bunny Levine at the 'Thelma' premiere in 2024. Amanda Edwards/Getty Images Bunny Levine, an actress who appeared in Gilmore Girls, You Don’t Mess With the Zohan, Thelma and numerous other TV shows and films, has died. She was 97. Levine died peacefully in her sleep, her manager confirmed to The Hollywood Reporter , with NBC Los Angeles reporting that she died Thursday at her home in Tarzana, California. Born on Dec. 22, 1928, in East Orange, New Jersey, Levine developed an interest in acting at a young age. But after graduating from high school, she put those dreams on hold for 25 years while working as a school librarian and raising her three children, according to her IMDB biography . After retiring, Levine began taking acting classes and auditioning for roles. Following the death of her husband, Bernard Levine, in 2003, she moved to Los Angeles. Related Stories Music Janie Bradford, "Money (That's What I Want)" Songwriter, Dies at 87 Movies Michael Wright, Star of 'The Five Heartbeats' and 'Sugar Hill,' Dies at 70 Levine went on to build an extensive résumé of television appearances, including roles on Law & Order, Everybody Loves Raymond, Gilmore Girls , Ugly Betty, Private Practice, Criminal Minds, 2 Broke Girls, Raising Hope, Southland, New Girl, Getting On, The Mindy Project, Fuller House, Shameless and Dave. Her film credits included Slime City, The Jimmy Show, A Thousand Words, La La Land and the Adam Sandler-starring comedy You Don’t Mess With the Zohan in 2008. Levine later reunited with Sandler for Sandy Wexler in 2017 and the 2023 Netflix film You Are So Not Invited to My Bat Mitzvah . Levine continued acting into her 90s. Her more recent credits include The Invisible Raptor (2023); Michael Angarano’s Sacramento (2024), starring Kristen Stewart and Michael Cera; and Thelma (2024), starring June Squibb . She also appeared in projects released this year, including the final season of The Upshaws and The Cure. THR

title: HollyShorts Festival Set To Propel Documentary Jury Award Winner Into Oscar Race
full_text: Skip to main content By Matthew Carey Matthew Carey Documentary Editor, Awards @mattcarey More Stories By Matthew Doc Talk Podcast: Rebecca Miller On Her Emmy-Nominated ‘Mr. Scorsese’, A Journey Into The Mind And Mastery Of Martin Scorsese DOC NYC Set To Honor Documentary Visionaries Alex Gibney, JT Takagi, Stephen Maing, And Raney Aronson-Rath Emmys Host Mariska Hargitay Shares Scoop On Help From Colbert Writers And Why Stars Could Make Cameos With ‘SUV’ Toe Tags View All August 22, 2026 2:23pm HollyShorts By the end of the weekend, another documentary short will have punched its ticket to the Oscar race. The 22nd HollyShorts , the prestigious film festival in Los Angeles, will announce jury award winners Sunday in multiple categories, with four of them qualifying for the Academy Awards: Best Short Film Grand Prize, Best Short Animation, Best Short Live Action, and Best Documentary Short. The nonfiction contenders constitute “one of its strongest documentary programs to date,” the festival notes, exploring a wide range of themes. Two of them center on stories of the formerly incarcerated: I Got My Brother , directed by Victor K. Gabriel, examines siblings Jarrett Harper and Baylon Harper, who were dealt a very tough hand of cards as infants. They were shuffled around L.A.’s foster care system, where they faced Dickensian conditions. Related Stories News 'Degree of Certainty' Filmmaker Simon Schneider Tackles The Ironic Origins Of Climate Change Data -- HollyShorts Film Festival News Renée Zellweger, Michael Keaton & Judi Dench Projects Make 2026 HollyShorts Lineup Jarrett Harper (right) and Baylon Harper in ‘I Got My Brother.’ L.A. Times/Breakwater Studios/Schultz Family Foundation Jarrett, the elder brother, was eventually taken in by a man who later abused him, a victimizer who then set his sights on Baylon. Fearing what would happen to his younger brother, Jarrett killed the man and was sentenced to life in prison without possibility of parole. Eventually, Gov. Jerry Brown of California commuted his sentence. I Got My Brother offers a surprisingly joyous portrait of the Harpers as their bond remains unshakeable after Jarrett’s release. Watch on Deadline Freddie Nole Sweet World Films The Second Life of Freddie Nole , directed by Dana Nachman, follows the titular Nole, who spent an astonishing 50 years in prison. When he ultimately got out, Nole was essentially dumped on the street by the prison system, without any resources. Determined not to let this happen to others in his circumstances, Nole founded Meeting at the Door, a nonprofit that offers free transportation, a restaurant meal, new clothes, a prepaid phone, and valuable advice to newly freed prisoners. (After watching the film, I immediately donated to Meeting at the Door). HollyShorts contender The Time My Grandmother Was Held Hostage by Bank Robbers , directed by Rosella Tursi, tells the extraordinary story of the filmmaker’s nonna (Italian for grandma), who was minding her own business one day in her home in Montreal in 1983 when two men fleeing after a bank holdup burst into her place and held her captive. Rosa Tursi in ‘The Time My Grandmother Was Held Hostage by Bank Robbers.’ Aspen Film The documentary interweaves the memories of family members – some alive at the time of the news making drama and others who heard it second hand as they grew up. Remarkably, after more than a 40-year interval, Tursi was able to track down one of the hostage takers to get his recollections of that fateful day. The film, which premiered at DOC NYC last November, is full of humor and wonderful details – like a historical disagreement over whether the bank robbers availed themselves of a beer from nonna Rosa’s refrigerator, or not a frosty brew but a Mountain Dew. What isn’t in dispute is that they graciously offered to reimburse Rosa for the beverage, perhaps out of their newly acquired wad of cash. Black Panther Party “cubs” in ‘When The Revolution Doesn’t Come.’ HollyShorts When The Revolution Doesn’t Come , directed by Aurora Brachman, takes a fascinating look at “Black Panther Party cubs” – that is to say, children of parents integral to the movement. Among them is the son of Fred Hampton, a senior leader of the Black Panther Party who was assassinated by the FBI in 1969, at the age of 21. Another figure in the film: Erika Brown-Abram, daughter of Elaine Brown, who was chairwoman of the Black Panther Party. The film examines how these children of Black Panther Party leaders – now adults – maintain the ideals and purpose of the movement when, as the title suggests, the revolution didn’t come as their parents had hoped. The documentary premiered in June at Tribeca Festival. Markus Füchtner with nutcracker in ‘The Chimney Sweeper.’ RiverRun International Film Festival The Chimney Sweeper , meanwhile, directed by Jack Raese, centers on Markus Füchtner, a woodcarver and descendant of William Füchtner, “known as the father of the nutcracker,” according to the Leavenworth Nutcracker Museum. The 19 th century Füchtner “made the first commercial production of nutcrackers” on a lathe, crafting “standing wooden nutcrackers in the form of soldiers and kings.” Why wouldn’t the film be titled The Nutcracker (or perhaps the German Nussknacker )? Well, it turns out Markus faced a bit of a crisis deciding whether to follow his great-great-great-grandfather into the nutcracker business, or head down a chimney with a brush. Those are just a few of the short docs in the HollyShorts lineup. It has also screened The Baddest Speech Writer of All , directed by two-time Oscar winner Ben Proudfoot, and Emily and Dave Schuman’s The Baker’s Hotline , which “offers a heartwarming look inside King Arthur Flour’s renowned baking helpline, where expert bakers forge unexpected human connections one phone call at a time.” Among eye-catching sport documentaries, HollyShorts notes, is ZINA , produced by Serena Williams, “shining a light on tennis pioneer Zina Garrison, revealing the triumphs and personal struggles behind one of the sport’s most influential yet overlooked champions.” Set Pace introduces Britain’s first Black female motorsport official as she launches her own race team. Miles of Life chronicles a former Ugandan runner “who channels personal disappointment into transforming his community,” while The Angry Bird , follows “female stock car racer Georgie´s fight to reclaim her place on the track following a devastating crash.” The 22 nd edition of HollyShorts opened August 13 and concludes on Sunday. The festival takes place at the TCL Chinese Theatres and venues throughout Ovation Hollywood. title: Dale Morris, Titan of Nashville Management Who Forged Superstar Careers for Kenny Chesney and Alabama, Dies at 89
full_text: Aug 22, 2026 2:00pm PT Dale Morris, Titan of Nashville Management Who Forged Superstar Careers for Kenny Chesney and Alabama, Dies at 89 By Chris Willman Plus Icon Chris Willman Senior Music Writer and Chief Music Critic ChrisWillman Latest Dale Morris, Titan of Nashville Management Who Forged Superstar Careers for Kenny Chesney and Alabama, Dies at 89 12 hours ago Olivia Rodrigo Releases ‘Handmaid’s Tale’-Inspired Song, ‘Serena Joy,’ in a Tiny Run of CDs, With Digital Drop to Follow 1 day ago The Hollies Officially Call It Quits, as Last Two Members of Classic 1960s Lineup Retire After Being in Band for 63 Years 2 days ago See All Rick Diamond Dale Morris, one of the leading names in the ranks of Nashville music managers, who helped build up superstar careers for the group Alabama and then Kenny Chesney nearly from scratch, died Friday at 89. A representative said Morris died in his sleep. “He lived a big, bold, beautiful, blessed life, and I’m holding onto that right now,” said his protege and eventually managerial partner of many years, Clint Higham, president of Morris Higham Management. “It’s the end of an era.” Related Stories China Box Office: 'Spider-Man: Brand New Day' Swings to Massive $121 Million Five-Day Opening China Box Office: 'Once Upon a Time in the Middle East' Dominates With $70 Million Weekend as Christopher Nolan's 'The Odyssey' Debuts Second Morris met the fledgling Alabama in 1979 while heading up Dale Morris & Associates and played a massive role in making the group the most successful band in the history of country music, with 33 No. 1 hits in the 1980s and ’90s, along with a huge touring career that led to their being named Entertainer of the Year three times by the Country Music Association and five times by the Academy of Country Music in the mid-’80s. Alabama’s meteoric rise saw the group being credited for being early in country music to adopt some of rock’s touring production values, finding rock-star-level success as well. Popular on Variety Lightning struck twice for Morris, as he oversaw the rise of Chesney from a country also-ran into the genre’s most reliable stadium-filler, who was named Entertainer of the Year four times in the 2000s by both the CMAs and ACMs, and who has enjoyed 32 No. 1 Billboard country smashes. Other artists Morris steered included Old Dominion, Ricky Van Shelton, Jerry Lee Lewis and his very first management client going back into the late ’60s, Bobby “Crash” Craddock. Said Higham, “He was larger than life, and never met a dream he couldn’t build. Dale Morris gave me my first internship, and I never wanted to go anywhere else. He saw things in people, in me, in Kenny, and inspired everyone to reach beyond what we thought possible. Maybe it’s how much he loved life, loved his family, loved us.” Chesney devoted significant passages in his 2025 book, “Heart Life Music,” to describing his relationship with Morris, which came about from him being a huge fan of Alabama and discovering there was a man behind the scenes making it happen. “By the time I came into Dale Morris’s orbit, he’d been to the top of the mountain with Alabama and redefined what was possible in country music,” Chesney wrote in his book, co-authored with Holly Gleason. “Alabama not only won all the awards, sold millions of albums, had iconic hit after iconic hit, they’d created a new mainstream country star who actually looked like their audience… Alabama was high energy, the drums were rock and roll; Jeff Cook played fancy guitars and Randy Owen’s voice had this believability.” Watching the band roll into town for a concert, as a fan, Chesney noticed “there had been a fifth person. A man with white hair, I figured might have been someone’s father. Over time, I realized their manager had been the one to see around corners, didn’t do business the way everyone else did, made a space for a band who’d shown up looking like their fans. He didn’t care about anything but getting the music to the fans—and that was me, standing in a field, waiting for Alabama to arrive.” Dale Morris Morris Higham Management When Chesney finally got the chance to meet with Morris as an aspiring artist, he said, the manager “also asked hard questions, really digging in on what it took… ‘How hard are you willing to work?’ ‘How far will you go when it’s so hard and it’s not happening?’ I would have said anything to get Dale Morris to manage me… “We talked about country music. Even more than Alabama, how songs and charisma were such a part of it, that spoke to country people,” Chesney continued. “He told me his story. The similarities emerged. He was from South Carolina, another small Southern town with heart and people who all knew one another. He worked hard, to build a life, to create something more. He’d been a salesman, and he had that used car salesman thing where he could slap you on the back, be a good ole boy like your best friend. “He loved music, made friends, some people thought he could be a manager. He started with Billy “Crash” Craddock, doing booking, picking up Jerry Lee Lewis. Successful, but he wanted something more. He’d seen a band in Myrtle Beach, who’d put out an independent record. They needed help. Dale applied himself. Once he and Alabama got going, they were in it together. When he realized arenas weren’t paying country acts like the rock bands, he took his band to the fields. Literally, set up a stage, charged a fair price for the fans, and tripled their money. … “Classy, grateful, and humble, he knew how to make deals and close. I had a friend who called him ‘Make a Deal Dale’,” Chesney wrote. “He was raw, too. No airs, just unfiltered honesty about how rough it could be. He had relationships with everybody: labels, radio stations, big promoters, TV people, and publishers, but also the fair buyers, the country bar owners, the folks out in America who held careers together. We were gonna need them even more. “I didn’t bother meeting with another manager. Dale loved the game, and he loved coming up with new ways to do it. If I was willing to work as hard as I said, maybe I was the kid who’d let him do it all over again. He didn’t believe in contracts. Didn’t have one with Alabama, didn’t need one with me. He said, ‘Let’s do it.'” Before taking on management, Morris began his career as a songwriter, reaching the top 5 in 1967 with a cut by Johnny Paycheck, “Don’t Monkey With Another Monkey’s Monkey.” He was inspired by that hit to move more into the business side, at first doing radio promo work for Little Darlin’ Records, before he joined producer Ron Chancey in starting Cartwheel Records. Their success with Billy “Crash” Craddock led resulted in ABC purchasing the label, which spurred Morris to move on to exploring management, starting International House of Talent, where he both managed and booked Craddock. It was a decade into his management career that he discovered Alabama, with an agency arm, Dale Morris & Associates, booking shows for the group and finding increasingly large venues that few country acts of the time were playing. As Alabama’s shows grew, Morris realized other needs created by the group’s growth and purchased Bob Seger’s sound system in order to found Morris Leasing, which later became Morris Lighting + Sound. In 2010, Morris was elected into the International Talent Buyers Association Hall of Fame. He received the T.J. Martell Foundation’s Tony Martell Lifetime Entertainment Achievement Award in 2014 (at which he is pictured holding his trophy alongside Chesney, at top). Higham rose to become Morris’ partner after starting as an intern. In 2018, the two of them sold their booking agency part of their company to Paradigm Talent Agency (now The-Team), while continuing to hold onto the management division. In an interview with Pollstar that year, Morris said, “We’ve elected to stay small rather than to try to sign every act in the world. That way we were able to do what we were able to do and book and manage. Everybody seemed to be happy. We never signed contracts with any of the acts we represented. You come with us and if you want to leave us tomorrow, pay us what you owe us and out the door you go. That’s been our policy for at least 45 years.” Morris was married to his wife, Earline, for 68 years. He was preceded in death by a son, Tim. Survivors include the couple’s daughter-in-law, Jennifer, grandchildren Zack, Colton (and wife Mary Blair), Nick (and wife Shelby) and Kendall, and great grandchildren Mary Dee and Gus. “We’re so blessed to have had 90 years with him as the patriarch of our family,” said Zack Morris. “Thank you to our music industry family and to his vast community of friends in Nashville, Boca and beyond for loving him all these many years.” A celebration of life is being planned for this fall, with details to be announced in the weeks ahead. title: ‘Sentimental Value’ Sweeps Amanda Awards
full_text: Aug 22, 2026 12:45pm PT ‘Sentimental Value’ Sweeps Amanda Awards ‘One Battle After Another’ was named best foreign film By Marta Balaga Plus Icon Marta Balaga Latest ‘Sentimental Value’ Sweeps Amanda Awards 13 hours ago Monica Bellucci Has ‘Never’ Done Anything Like ‘Ketticè’: ‘I Was on Set in My Pajamas With a Knife in My Hand and Slippers on My Feet’ 2 weeks ago Olivia Wilde Calls ‘The Invite’ the ‘Most Incredible’ Experience of Her Life: ‘It Was the Highlight of My Career’ 2 weeks ago See All 'Sentimental Value'. Kasper Tuxen/Mubi Joachim Trier ’s Oscar winner “ Sentimental Value ” became this year’s biggest Amanda Awards winner, taking home eight statuettes, including the top prize for best Norwegian film. Trier was also awarded for directing, as well as his screenplay written with longtime collaborator Eskil Vogt. “There’s a lot of stuff going on when you make and release films, and we both like to go back to that safe space and rediscover that calm where it’s just our two voices. We are fortunate enough that our films generate more and more noise that we have to shut out, so when we work, we make it personal and small again,” they told Variety back in January. Related Stories China Box Office: 'Spider-Man: Brand New Day' Swings to Massive $121 Million Five-Day Opening China Box Office: 'Once Upon a Time in the Middle East' Dominates With $70 Million Weekend as Christopher Nolan's 'The Odyssey' Debuts Second “When I write alone, I procrastinate. When I’m procrastinating with Joachim, even if I haven’t done anything, at least I got to spend a day with my friend,” said Vogt, with Trier adding: “Eskil is my longest relationship outside of my parents. We don’t need to be silly romantic about it, but we have to be honest: it’s a real gift.” Popular on Variety Paul Thomas Anderson’s hit “ One Battle After Another ” tok home the Amanda For best foreign film. On the acting front, Pia Tjelta scored her second Amanda – this time for her performance in “Don’t Call Me Mama.” Inga Ibsdotter Lilleaas won for “Sentimental Value,” while Anna Drakopoulou Sverrisdóttir was named Newcomer of the Year for “Brightly Shining.” “The Battle of Oslo” – last year’s opening film at the Norwegian International Film Festival Haugesund – won the People’s Amanda. It depicts the sinking of German cruiser Blücher, under the leadership of Colonel Birger Eriksen, and “is one of the most famous events in our history. Some people are calling it the single most important event during the WWII in Norway,” said director Daniel Fahre. “We kept it quite accurate, also because it’s such a thrilling story. But we had to look for its emotional side, because there’s no mention of that in military reports. I am sure Colonel Eriksen had doubts, that he was afraid. But nobody wrote about it. I wanted to follow the facts and see what was hiding behind them.” The Amanda Committee’s Honorary Award went to Per Christian Ellefsen, known for “Elling” and called by the jurors “one of Norway’s most beloved actors.” “The first film about Elling was released in 2001, meaning it celebrates its 25th anniversary this year, and Per Christian Ellefsen was nominated for an Amanda Award for the title role in the first film,” they recalled, saying that “few characters in Norwegian cinema have been as beloved.” “While he struggles through three successful films, Per Christian Ellefsen certainly masters the role of Elling to perfection,” they said. Finally, the Amanda Committee’s Golden Clapper went to casting directirs Mette Holme Nielsen and Jannecke Bervell for their contributions to Norwegian film over more than 30 years. “Casting is one of the most crucial elements in film and TV production, yet it is also one of the most underrated. It is in the casting process that the script meets the actors, and this is where the foundation for credibility, chemistry, and cohesion is laid,” argued the jury. “A good casting can elevate an entire production, while poor casting can bring a film down. Casting also plays an important role in promoting diversity, by opening the doors to new voices, new expressions and a broader range of people on screen. It is therefore a profession that requires instinct, an understanding of people, experience and the ability to see potential where others may not.” Mette Holme Nielsen is known for “Kitchen Stories” and “Utøya July 22,” which earned her a nomination for the International Casting Director Award. Jannecke Bervell worked on “Elling,” “Kon-Tiki” or “The Quake.” The Amanda Awards were hosted by Vegard Larsen and Linnea Myhre. The broadcast was produced by Monster for NRK. title: Before ‘The Pitt,’ There Was ‘St. Elsewhere’
full_text: × Skip to main content By Rick Porter Plus Icon Rick Porter Television Business Editor rickporter Follow Sign Up View All August 22, 2026 11:30am From left: Ed Begley Jr., Cindy Pickett, Bruce Greenwood, David Morse and Denzel Washington on St. Elsewhere, which ran from 1982 to 1988 and won six Emmys in 1986. Courtesy Everett Collection Though it was never an outright hit, St. Elsewhere punched way above its weight in terms of the careers it helped launch and a style that set the template for medical dramas that followed it. The show can also boast one of the more memorable series finales in TV history. Created by Joshua Brand and John Falsey, St. Elsewhere followed the staff and patients at a struggling Boston hospital over six seasons on NBC, from 1982 to 1988. Like its fellow NBC show Hill Street Blues (both were from MTM Enterprises), St. Elsewhere pioneered a new kind of storytelling. Hospital dramas that came before it focused mainly on a lead character whose personal struggles didn’t interfere with their work and presented the health care system as orderly and well functioning (see Marcus Welby, M.D. , Trapper John, M.D. ). St. Elsewhere instead took a grittier tack, with overlapping, serialized stories and medical professionals who had complicated lives and sometimes could not save patients ­— traits that are recognizable in its successors, from ER to Grey’s Anatomy to The Pitt . Related Stories 'Awards Chatter' Podcast Emmy Nominee Patrick Ball on His Rollercoaster Journey to 'The Pitt' and How His Own Addiction Battle Has Informed His Performance TV 'Palm Royale' Went Full 'Dynasty' for Its Biggest Fight Yet When the series debuted, that style was seen as a barrier to success: Reviewing the show in November 1982, THR critic Richard Hack wrote, “So real and graphic is the drama being presented here that we cannot believe that 20 million people across this country will find it entertaining enough to flip to.” Nonetheless, St. Elsewhere would win 13 Emmys over its run, including six for its fourth season in 1986. It was nominated for best drama series in all six seasons, though it never took home that honor. Three of the show’s regulars — William Daniels, Bonnie Bartlett and Ed Flanders — won acting Emmys for their roles. Equally impressive was the show’s eye for emerging talent: It helped kick-start the careers of Denzel Washington, Mark Harmon and David Morse, as well as comedian Howie Mandel, playing against type in a dramatic role. The 1988 series finale cemented St. Elsewhere ’s place in TV lore by suggesting that the entire show may have taken place inside the imagination of Tommy Westphall (played by Chad Allen), the autistic son of Flanders’ Dr. Donald Westphall. It was perhaps the most audacious choice an already groundbreaking show ever made. This story first appeared in an August stand-alone issue of The Hollywood Reporter magazine. title: Why Do We Love Spider-Man So Much?
full_text: Aug 22, 2026 11:02am PT Why Do We Love Spider-Man So Much? By Owen Gleiberman Plus Icon Owen Gleiberman Chief Film Critic @OwenGleiberman Latest Why Do We Love Spider-Man So Much? 15 hours ago ‘Spa Weekend’ Review: Leslie Mann and Isla Fisher in a High-Concept Comedy Without the Comic Highs 1 day ago ‘Mutiny’ Review: Jason Statham Dies Hard on a Cargo Ship in a Thriller of Impeccable Bring-the-Pain Timing 4 days ago See All ©Sony Pictures/Courtesy Everett Collection Why does everyone love Spider-Man so much? When “Spider-Man: No Way Home” came out at the end of 2021, it made an insane amount of money ($814 million in the U.S. alone), blasting away any vestige of that era’s comic-book-movie fatigue. I thought the reason for the film’s mind-boggling success was obvious: It had three Spider-Men in it — Tom Holland , Andrew Garfield, and the OG Tobey Maguire — and that made it a unique royal-family reunion of spider-veined spandex. Related Stories China Box Office: 'Once Upon a Time in the Middle East' Dominates With $70 Million Weekend as Christopher Nolan's 'The Odyssey' Debuts Second China Box Office: 'Spider-Man: Brand New Day' Swings to Massive $121 Million Five-Day Opening There was a perfect storm of happenstance to how that confluence came to be. “Spider-Man: Into the Spider-Verse” (an infinitely better movie) had come out two years before, and borrowing deeply from the comic books it did a brilliant job of injecting head-spinning multiverse madness into the Spider-Man saga. The makers of “No Way Home” said, in essence, “Let’s do the same thing — only in a pandering, overstuffed, how-many-movie-stars-can-dangle-from-the-end-of-a-web? way.” I thought it was the definition of a one-shot. Popular on Variety But “ Spider-Man: Brand New Day ” has rewritten the playbook again. The movie is a solid and well-executed adventure, no more and no less, in which Holland’s Peter Parker and his love, MJ (Zendaya), barely even get to talk (because she doesn’t remember who she is). No one is pretending that “Brand New Day” is as great as, say, “Spider-Man 2.” Yet despite that, it is now likely to become… the top-grossing movie of all time . At least until the next Spider-Man adventure comes along. Why Spider-Man, why now? Ever since his debut in 1962, he has been immensely popular (though Stan Lee had to fight a skeptical publisher to approve the character). But if you look back over 50 years of American comic-book-movie culture, it’s undeniable that the two reigning superheroes have been Superman and Batman. Christopher Reeve’s performance in the first two “Superman” films remains, to me (and many others) , the most perfect live-action embodiment of a superhero there has ever been. Those first two films loom mythologically. After that, it was Batman who ruled for decades as the comic-book-movie antihero of our age. Batman is, of course, the only superhero who possesses no superpowers, which makes him uniquely like us. (With a bit more attitude, we feel like we could be him.) He’s the brooding cool film-noir god of the existential night who speaks to our alienation, which is why Christopher Nolan’s “ The Dark Knight ” is the greatest comic-book movie ever made. And let’s not underestimate the original creationist jolt given to live-action superhero culture by the indelible “Batman” TV series of the late ’60s. In half-hour episodes shot on cruddy sets, that show achieved the uncanny sense of being a comic book come to life. Adam West’s performance conveyed gravitas with a wry wink that’s never been matched. Does sweet, genial, wholesomely sexy Tom Holland really compete with all of that? Holland has grown in confidence as an actor, and there’s no doubt that he now owns the role of Peter Parker even more than Tobey Maguire did (Garfield, stuck in a sub-par chapter of the franchise, always looked glum and a bit lost). A generation has grown up with Holland, and now that his Peter is a young adult, he seems poised to rule all the more. One reason that superhero fatigue is always lingering around the corner is that the very quality that attracts us to comic-book superheroes — their Olympian strength and majesty, their pumped iconography of invincibility — is also, in an underlying way, exhausting. More and more, they come at us jam-packed into teams: the Avengers, the X-Men, the Fantastic Four. How super can a hero really be when the world is lined with them? Spider-Man provides a cathartic relief from all that, coalescing around the keyword that almost everyone uses to describe him: relatability . Peter Parker, as we all know, starts off as an ordinary high schooler contending with the effects of a spider bite as if they were the onset of puberty. (He has to harness and control the act of shooting sticky webs out of his wrist.) He’s got bully problems, girlfriend problems, as well as secretly sensitive hidden-identity problems. He’s the James Dean of superheroes (the web-swinging crime fighter as misunderstood kid), and the way Holland embodies him, with a buff abashment just this side of shy, he’s like a boy-band star audiences want to cuddle up with. He also sticks to his home turf of New York City (he needs its canyons to swing), and to the comrades who surround him like family. In an all-superhero-politics-is-local way, that’s a crucial part of his relatability. Yet Peter, as a young adult, also strikes a special balance that speaks to us right now. In 1978, a scruffy but ultimately more optimistic time, the character of Superman kicked off comic-book-movie culture by being valiant, chiseled, indomitable, supreme. A decade later, as the glittery ’80s were starting to crash and burn, Batman arrived to take center stage: a wealthy player who had a hidden dark side, a gruff manner, and a “power” that was a grand illusion. His real power had to come from within. Spider-Man is the superhero for our time because he’s the perfect spiritual fusion of Superman and Batman. He wears all-American red-and-blue spandex and does an exhilarating version of flying around; he’s an Eagle Scout believer in his own destiny. But he’s also masked and furtive and traumatized. In “Brand New Day,” when his spidery abilities get discombobulated, he literally doesn’t know which end is up. And that makes him a mirror of how so many of us feel in these scary days of American turmoil: yearning to stand up to the darkness, yet also mired in it. In the “Spider-Verse” films, which are every bit as amazing (as cinema) as Spider-Man himself, he grapples with issues of identity that make Batman’s look like child’s cosplay. Who is Spider-Man? He’s the light and dark sides of comic-book culture poured into one. He’s the superhero who speaks to our anxieties and our dreams, the romantic teen idol who has to keep figuring out who he is. He makes us all feel like we’re hanging — thrillingly — by a thread. title: Janie Bradford, “Money (That’s What I Want)” Songwriter, Dies at 87
full_text: Skip to main content By Mike Barnes Plus Icon Mike Barnes Senior Editor mikebarnes4 Follow Sign Up View All August 22, 2026 10:02am Janie Bradford Leon Bennett/Getty Images Janie Bradford, the onetime receptionist for Berry Gordy who co-wrote the R&B classic “Money (That’s What I Want),” the first big hit for the founder of Motown Records, has died. She was 87. Bradford died Friday at Cedars-Sinai Medical Center in Los Angeles after an extended illness, her family announced. Bradford also co-wrote “Too Busy Thinking About My Baby,” which Marvin Gaye took to No. 4 on the Billboard Hot 100 in 1969, and songs for other artists including Mary Wells, Stevie Wonder, The Temptations, the Four Tops and Martha & the Vandellas. Related Stories Movies Michael Wright, Star of 'The Five Heartbeats' and 'Sugar Hill,' Dies at 70 Movies Paul M. Pollard, Camera Man on 'Bound for Glory' and 'Heaven's Gate,' Dies at 84 She later served as head of writer relations for the Motown publishing company Jobete. Born on June 2, 1939, in Charleston, Missouri, Bradford was inspired to be a writer after her idol, poet Robert Frost, visited her high school. While living in Detroit with her sister, Clea, she became neighborhood friends with singer Jackie Wilson, who had just charted with his first solo single, the 1957 party anthem “Reet Petite.” Wilson invited her to meet Gordy, one of the song’s writers, and she gave him a collection of her poetry. After Gordy had launched the Tamla and Motown labels in 1959, he hired Bradford as a receptionist. One day, as Gordy was working on a song, Bradford joined him at the piano to add her own verse — “Your love gives me such a thrill, but your love don’t pay my bills. Gimme some money, baby!” The song, of course, would become “Money (That’s What I Want).” First recorded by Barrett Strong, it peaked at No. 23 on the Hot 100 and helped cement Tamla/Motown as hit-makers. It would be covered by The Beatles, The Rolling Stones, The Flying Lizards, The Supremes, Boyz II Men and Charli XCX, among many others. “Janie was there with me from the very beginning, before there was even a Motown, and she will always hold a very special place in my heart and in the Motown family,” Gordy said in a statement. “Janie was smart, clever, witty and fun. She was also talented and determined. In those early days, everybody did what was needed to be done, and Janie was no exception. She became Motown’s first receptionist, but her talents quickly took her far beyond that desk.” Bradford’s credits also included “Contract on Love,” recorded by Little Stevie Wonder, Wells’ “Your Old Standby,” Diana Ross’s “I Am Me” and The Supremes’ “Time Changes Things” and “We Should Be Closer Together.” After some 25 years at Motown, Bradford in the 1990s founded the Heroes and Legends Awards, an event that over 30 years honored music icons and presented scholarships to those pursuing higher education. “Her annual gatherings always felt like old home week because Janie kept that wonderful sense of family alive,” Gordy said. In June, she was inducted into the Women Songwriters Hall of Fame. Survivors include her husband of 55 years, Wardean; her children, Lance and Nicole; her daughter-in-law, Carolyn; and her grandsons, Bradford and Austin. THR

title: ‘Spider-Man: Brand New Day’ Swinging to Fourth Box Office Victory as It Tops ‘Insidious’ Sequel
full_text: × Skip to main content By Ryan Gajewski Plus Icon Ryan Gajewski Senior Entertainment Reporter View All August 22, 2026 8:55am Tom Holland stars in 'Spider-Man: Brand New Day.' Sony Pictures Logo text Spider-Man: Brand New Day continues to deliver in its fourth weekend at the box office as it faces off against newcomers Insidious: Out of the Further and the Jason Statham -led Mutiny . Sony Pictures ‘ releases are set to claim the top two spots at the domestic box office, as Spider-Man: Brand New Day grossed $9.8 million on Friday, with the studio projecting it to add $36.5 million for the weekend amid its historic run . This would bring its domestic cume to $852.4 million through Sunday, surpassing 2021’s Spider-Man: No Way Home to become the No. 3 highest-grossing film ever at the domestic box office. This will also put Brand New Day as Sony’s highest-grossing domestic film after it set the record last weekend for the top global release in the studio’s history. Related Stories Beyond the Book How 'The Magic Faraway Tree' Embraced Its Dated Source Material to Deliver a Humble Yet Epic Adaptation Movies 'Insidious: Out of the Further' Hunts Down $3M in Box Office Previews Insidious: Out of the Further occupies second place with $10.6 million on Friday, including Thursday previews . Sony projects an opening weekend of $23.7 million for the sixth installment in the horror franchise that hails from Screen Gems , Stage 6 Films and Blumhouse Atomic Monster and kicked off with 2011’s original Insidious . Out of the Further earned a C+ CinemaScore, tying 2023’s Insidious: The Red Door for the series’ lowest grade. Debuting in 3,330 North American theaters, Out of the Further stars Amelia Eve, Brandon Perea and Lin Shaye and centers on a young mother who can bring spirits back with her to the real world. It follows The Red Door , which saw the return of original series stars Patrick Wilson and Rose Byrne. That one opened to an impressive $33 million domestically before grossing $189 million worldwide throughout its run. Amelia Eve in Insidious: Out of the Further. Sony Pictures With an $18 million production budget, Out of the Further holds a 60 percent approval rating from critics on Rotten Tomatoes and a 70 percent audience score. Critic Frank Scheck wrote in his review for The Hollywood Reporter that the film “proves routine in its elaborate plot machinations.” Also opening this weekend is Mutiny , as Lionsgate’s film notched $2.8 million domestically on Friday, including Thursday previews. Earning a B+ CinemaScore from audiences, Statham’s latest action title looks to pick up $7.4 million for the frame to land in sixth place from 2,600 North American screens. MadRiver Pictures and Punch Palace Productions produced the project that carries a $40 million production budget. Director Jean-François Richet’s feature stars Statham as a former Marine who sets out to prove his innocence after getting framed for murder. It holds a 50 percent approval score from critics on Rotten Tomatoes but an 80 percent score from audiences. Mutiny follows Statham’s Shelter , which opened with $5.5 million domestically earlier this year for Black Bear. Jason Statham as Cole Reed in Mutiny. Dan Smith/Lionsgate Universal’s The Odyssey is finding a home in third place with an estimated $18.5 million for its sixth weekend to bring its domestic total to $538 million. Starring Matt Damon as Odysseus, Christopher Nolan’s mythological epic surpassed Deadpool & Wolverine during the week to stand as the highest-grossing R-rated title globally. In its sophomore frame, director David Robert Mitchell’s dinosaur-focused The End of Oak Street looks to scarf down around $8 million to bring the Warner Bros. release’s two-week domestic total to $37 million. Anne Hathaway and Ewan McGregor star in the survival feature, which is set to decline by around 62 percent. The weekend’s top-earning dinosaur film has yet to be determined, as PAW Patrol : The Dino Movie is battling with The End of Oak Street for fourth place. Also in its second weekend, Paramount Pictures’ animated sequel is similarly targeting roughly $8 million to decline around 61 percent and bring its domestic tally to an estimated $34 million. Expanding to a wide release in its third weekend is A24’s Tony , starring Dominic Sessa as a teenage Anthony Bourdain. The feature serves up an estimated $4.8 million from 1,600 North American screens to claim seventh place and bring its domestic cume to around $6.4 million. The 25th-anniversary rerelease of Universal’s The Fast and the Furious pulls into eighth place with an estimated $3.3 million. The Vin Diesel vehicle grossed $207 million globally in its initial run to kick off the franchise that has a long-awaited eleventh installment in the works . Black Bear’s comedy Spa Weekend is currently in ninth place with an estimated $3 million domestically from 2,000 locations. Earning a B+ CinemaScore, directors Jon Lucas and Scott Moore’s movie stars Leslie Mann, Isla Fisher, Michelle Buteau and Anna Faris. Starring Andrew Garfield , The Magic Faraway Tree is heading for an estimated $1.15 million from 1,600 North American screens to land on the outskirts of the top 10. Vertical releases director Ben Gregor’s literary adaptation that also stars Claire Foy. Director Destin Daniel Cretton ‘s blockbuster Spider-Man: Brand New Day keeps spinning to historic heights. Tom Holland , Zendaya , Sadie Sink and Jon Bernthal star in the film that recently set the record as the fastest movie to hit $800 million domestically . After the weekend is over, only 2015’s Star Wars: Episode VII — The Force Awakens and 2019’s Avengers: Endgame will hold bigger domestic cumes. THR

title: Michael Wright, Star of ‘The Five Heartbeats’ and ‘Sugar Hill,’ Dies at 70
full_text: Skip to main content By Mike Barnes Plus Icon Mike Barnes Senior Editor mikebarnes4 Follow Sign Up View All August 22, 2026 8:18am Michael Wright Mark Von Holden/WireImage Michael Wright, who starred as the lead vocalist Eddie King Jr. in Robert Townsend’s The Five Heartbeats and as Wesley Snipes’ brother in Sugar Hill , has died. He was 70. Wright died Wednesday in Los Angeles of heart failure and complications from Marchiafava-Bignami disease, a rare degenerative neurological disorder, TMZ reported . “Our family is grieving an enormous and deeply personal loss,” his wife, Susan, wrote on Instagram. “Michael, your work will live forever, but your love will live even longer in the hearts of those who knew you best. Rest peacefully, my love. You will be missed beyond words.” Related Stories Movies Paul M. Pollard, Camera Man on 'Bound for Glory' and 'Heaven's Gate,' Dies at 84 Music Frank Beard, ZZ Top Drummer, Dies at 77 The lanky Wright also stood out as the Resistance fighter Elias Taylor on the popular NBC miniseries and series V in the mid-1980s and as the drug-addled inmate Omar White on 22 episodes of HBO’s Oz over three seasons from 2001-03. In The Five Heartbeats (1991), written by Townsend and Keenen Ivory Wayans, Wright sparkled as the leader of the Motown-inspired R&B group that struggles to deal with success over the years (his King character battled drugs and alcohol). The group also featured Townsend as Duck Matthews, Tico Wells as Anthony “Choirboy” Stone, Leon as J.T. Matthews and Harry J. Lennix as Terrence “Dresser” Williams. Wright was excellent again as Raynathan Skuggs, brother of Snipes’ Roemello Skuggs, in the gritty Sugar Hill (1994), written by Barry Michael Cooper in the second film of his “Harlem Trilogy.” From left: Leon, Robert Townsend, Tico Wells, Harry J. Lennix and Michael Wright in ‘The Five Heartbeats.’ 20th Century Fox Film / courtesy Everett Collection Wright was born in New York City on April 30, 1956. His mother, Alberta, owned Jezebel, a Southern restaurant in the theater district, and that’s where he met Townsend for the first time. “I never go out,” Townsend told New York magazine in 1991. “But before I knew it, we were club-hopping. Then we ended up in Michael’s apartment at 3 a.m. watching this Japanese film [ Bedtime Lies ] he’d made.” Wright had started out in a work study program at the Lee Strasberg Institute, where he “mopped floors, I answered phones, I did all kinds of tasks in exchange for my classes,” he told Sheen magazine in a 2021 interview. He then appeared in his first film as Clinton, the leader of The Del Bombers gang, in The Wanderers (1979), directed by Philip Kaufman, followed by a turn as a volatile young soldier named Carlyle in Robert Altman ’s Streamers (1983). Six months after their first meeting, Townsend sent him the script for The Five Heartbeats for the role that had been designed with Denzel Washington in mind. He noted that after Cooper had written the part of Raynathan for him in Sugar Hill , he was sitting in a coffee shop in Manhattan when Snipes walked in “with an entourage of about 10 people.” “I just stood up and got him by the lapels and said, ‘Man, I got a movie and I want you to make it with me,’” he said. “He wanted me to tell him more about it. We got in his limo. Wesley had a three-picture deal with Fox, I think. I got Wes to commit to making that film. That’s how that film got made. “That was an authentic New York role, and it was made for me. A lot of it was commiserate with my own personal journey. I improvised the whole film.” Wright’s résumé also included the films The Principal (1987), Money Talks (1997), Piñero (2001), The Interpreter (2005) and Dope King (2025) and the TV series Miami Vice , New York Undercover and Black Lightning . Survivors include five children and a grandchild. “The greatest sin an actor can commit is to fail to be interesting,” he said in his Sheen interview. “I always try to make my characters interesting. I want you to be riveted and wonder what’s going on behind my eyes. I want the audience to think along with me and go on an internal journey.” View this post on Instagram THR
